> Well, when I say 'A short history' it really means Quick, dirty, and very general.

Some of the Label history, and White units is covered in the "Zgrass Computer Expansion, A Longer history..." section.

After the JS&A mail order exclusive, Bally decided that some people might be afraid of the COMPUTER in the name plate. Thia caused 2 new name plates to be created.

Bally|Professional Arcade and Bally|Computer System

The Pro Arcade plate went on all the single units sold. The Computer system label was only seen in promotional pictures of white units on top of the Keyboard. I seems that this label was to go with game units sold with a keyboard.

Near the end of Bally's, direct involvement with the arcade, they started selling off the White units with the Pro Arcade covers. Then later still started selling the regular and white units with the Computer system labels.

When Astrovision took over, they had a supply of Pro Arcade labels, Large supply of Computer system labels, and a contract that said they only had a limited time to use the Bally name. So Atrovision boxes mostly have Computer systems in them. but Pro Arcades can be found.

When it came time for the name change on the units,(we recently discovered) they intended to go with 'Astro|The Professional Arcade" however at the same time they discovered there name 'Astrovision' also belonged to an older co. in the TV video electronics field.

This caused the name change to 'Astrocade'. I can only guess why the system changed also. Maybe 'Astro Boy' or 'Astro' the Jetsons dog? either way the unit also changed to 'Astrocade'.

However the double name change and aborted marketing for the original name change caused much financial drain on Astrocade. So, when there supply of the 'Astrocade' labels (both bottom and top I'm surmising) ran out, they just grabed whatever labels they still had in stock. So, Astrocade boxes mostly still have 'Computer system' labels with some 'Pro arcade' and rarest of them 'Astrocade'.

As for a 'Pro Arcade' label on an Astrovision unit making it rarer, maybe, technically, but as there is no difference in the actual hardware per say, and any one can swap any common label with any common base. It makes no difference.

In fact, warranty repairs (In Canada at least) involved them giving you a new base with your old cover. So a Bally base would change to an Astrovision base, but retain the 'Pro Arcade' name plate.

That's several questions, which I'll answer in turn.

On testing:

As far as seeing how it runs in the emulator: any chance some of you
could test that end of things for me? Without releasing the current
images to the public, until we decide on which one is the best one to
release? I haven't used that emu in years, and you guys presumably use
it often: you'd be much more aware of small differences and the like.

If I still had a real Bally system I'd just burn multiple copies of it
on something like 2716 EPROMs, and try them on the real thing. My only
working Bally system fried itself, years ago. So -- I'm willing to burn
multiple copies of the thing(s), and send them on 2716 EPROMs to Mike
White. Mike could then real-life-test each of them, and scan through
the code, to decide as to which one is the best release candidate of
our current bunch. (Assuming I get no further differences, that is.)

On re-dumping:

I'll re-dump it as often as needed; no worries there. I doubt Adam is
any big hurry to get the board / chip back, either. He and I are both
fans of the data / information being good, rather than worrying about
the actual hardware's cosmetic condition or whatever. Most of the 130+
carts I've dumped over the years, for various systems, I sold off or
traded relatively quickly ... in part to obtain more carts to dump.

As far as eliminating variables goes: I'm not dumping a cart; just the
2516 chip, itself -- thereby eliminating variables with the PC board
and the adapting device that I'd be using, if I were dumping a cart. I
just have a PC board with a socket, plus the 2516 chip. I gently pulled
the chip out of the socket, and dropped it right into the Promenade C1
device that I have always used as my "old chip" reader and writer,
after cleaning and straightening the legs. And one thing I always do,
once the ZIF (zero insertion force) socket's lever is closed, is to
sort of wiggle or slide the chip from side to side: thereby making sure
the chip's legs and the ZIF socket make good contact, electrically.

As far as damage to that chip goes: one leg must have broken off, a
bunch of years ago. Someone had soldered a replacement leg onto it. Far
as I can tell, that works fine: just looks non-factory. (I've done a
number of similar repairs on other chips, over the years.)

I was initially worried when I saw a 20-plus-year-old EPROM chip, with
no covering over the window area -- but from the sound of it, the thing
spent most of its life in a covered box of some kind or other: thereby
cutting down on any light that may have accidentally erased the data,
otherwise. It has a cover on it now, to help preserve the data.

On instability:

The 2516 chip itself is not being too terribly flaky on me: I think
that most of the difference in dumping results is my fault, not the
chip's fault. A half-erased chip would presumably be stable when it got
dumped; so I'm blaming any instability on my being out of practice,
after five years of not dumping anything. Keep in mind that some level
of instability or initial flakiness is normal, in my experience. In the
past I just kept dumping stuff until I was sure it was all kosher.

Conclusion:

While I will gladly redump it, I suggest we wait for a while before we
do that. Reason is simple: I need more "getting un-rusty" practice.

That's going to happen, soonish: Lance just snail mailed me an entire
new-to-me console (the APF MP-1000) with a bunch of carts. (Not here
yet, but hopefully soon.) Also, I want to solder up an adapter cable,
to start dumping Arcadia 2001 console family carts, if/when any new
ones become available and the owners decide to do a cart loan to me. In
the meantime (diminishing returns on the Arcadia's library) I'm going
to re-dump some of the 20 or so common carts I have for that system,
for two reasons: practice, plus checking for any minor differences.

  -- Ward Shrake --

I worked on that EPROM again, tonight ... and the second dump of the
2516 chip that contained "Fawn Dungeon" is now officially the official
one.  ;-)  I vouch for that second dump now, fully ... so delete the
first one, Paul and Adam ... and when you're ready, release that pup!

For those that are interested in this sort of thing ... first day's
attempt at reading that chip (as I said before, on one board or other)
was flaky enough that I didn't even save the data. I figured I was just
rusty; and it'd come back to me with a bit more practice. (It did.) I
saved the second one; and Adam confirmed what it was, and so forth. Out
of an abundance of caution / healthy excess of paranoia, I dumped it a
few more times, on a third day ... and came up with two bytes that read
differently, towards the end of the data. Paul was kind enough to test
both of the archived programs for me, and report back (publicly, here)
saying the second dump looked to be the more reliably working one.

All that's known. Tonight, I worked on the chip's legs in a number of
ways, in an attempt to get a more stable read. Thanks to that work, the
chip never once read as anything but the second dump. I read it six or
eight times; taking it out of the Promenade C1 reader/writer I love so
much, after each read, and letting the Promenade read "empty air" ...
and then putting it back in, and reading it again, for another cycle.
The "Promos 2.0" software gives a checksum and a hashtotal for every
read; so it would go from $FE and $34 (chip inserted) or $00 and $00
(empty air), over and over. Doesn't get any more reliable than that!

The reads are now so consistent and stable that I've set the EPROM
aside temporarily, so I can use it as a control EPROM: in other words,
as a chip I can count on to tell me what I want to hear -- thereby
telling me that the Promenade isn't flaking out, and neither am I. I
can then insure that everything's kosher, as I do future archiving.

This next part's included not so much as a brag or anything; but for
those who don't do much soldering or hardware repair work, but find
that sort of process to be of interest. (Adam's quickly becoming Mr.
Solder Guy ... so he may enjoy this, Hopefully, others will too.)


The stuff I did to the chip's legs boils down to gently straightening
each leg, in all directions; then gently sanding the skinny edges or
sides of each leg, using doubled-over sandpaper I use with my scale
modeling hobby activities (see "Internet Modeler" for articles I wrote,
from about August 2007 to present) -- that particular work done because
my Promenade machine's ZIF (zero insertion force) socket grabs that
part instead of the much wider flat surfaces -- and then I
carefully "tinned" each leg, using very thin gauge silver-bearing
solder that Radio Shack sells; and then carefully removed all but a
thin coating of that solder, from all four sides of each leg. (Days ago
I had cleaned the two fat, flat surfaces of each leg using a big pink
rubber eraser: it's a gentle way to get rid of minor contaminants.)

That's sort of standard stuff, for picky carts or chips ...  but not
usually done unless testing proves a cart needs more help than most.

The one thing that may have helped me more was desoldering a previous
repair; making sure all of that old solder (which was a dark grey in
color: not good!) was removed, by adding more of the good solder and
then removing most of it; and repeating that, several (three?) times.
I'm not sure why that works so well, but sometimes it helps a lot. It
could be some of the flux chemicals, removing oxides and other junk.

I then did a fairly straight-forward-but-somewhat-advanced repair: in
essence, I made a new leg to replace one that was missing. A section of
26 gauge, single-strand wire was partially stripped; then partially
tinned. I bent it around the chip, so that the tinned section was near
the area I wanted it to be attached to: with the rest of the wire just
there because it's a heck of a lot easier to control the repair work if
you can get your fingers around a part, instead of using tweezers. I
put the work in a third-hand holding device (with the alligator clips
holding the excess wire onto the chip, reasonably tightly). I used a
small screwdriver to apply gentle pressure to another portion of the
wire that wasn't in my way; and then heated the two parts for a few
seconds, using a temperature-controlled Weller soldering station.

I sort of wicked most of the excess solder along the wire and away from
the important repair area; then let it cool down for a few minutes. 
(Sort of like a kid wiping his nose on his sleeve; except with solder.)
The final step was to carefully cut the wire down to its final length,
using some sharp wire strippers that also work like strong scissors.

I sent some work-in-progress photos to Adam and Paul, that show some of
that work in a more visually friendly way. Not sure when/if it'll end
up at the Bally Alley web site ... but I presume it'll show up there.

Anyway ... Fawn Dungeon's official now; and I can proceed with my other
archiving work, on the APF MP-1000 and Arcadia 2001 game consoles.

5446:
Well, there are different levels of emulator programming.  Some of the
work people do, like breaking encryption and reverse engineering
custom chips, is truly astounding.  What I did was to take some of
MESS's control macros and arrange them in a more sensible way.  For
example, the original code to set up the player 1 knob was:

PORT_BIT( 0xff, 0x00, IPT_PADDLE) PORT_SENSITIVITY(85)
PORT_KEYDELTA(20) PORT_MINMAX(0,255) PORT_CODE_DEC(KEYCODE_X)
PORT_CODE_INC(KEYCODE_Z) PORT_PLAYER(1)

PORT_KEYDELTA sets the default speed when faking analog input with the
keyboard (which I don't recommend).  20 moved so far with a single
button press as to be practically unplayable, so I reduced it to 10.
By default, a paddle in MESS autocenters, which makes no sense for an
Astrocade controller.  So, I added the PORT_CENTERDELTA macro and set
it to zero.  Finally, the paddle was moving in the wrong direction, so
I set PORT_INVERT and flipped the digital inputs.  So, this line becomes:

PORT_BIT( 0xff, 0x00, IPT_PADDLE) PORT_INVERT PORT_SENSITIVITY(85)
PORT_KEYDELTA(10) PORT_CENTERDELTA(0) PORT_MINMAX(0,255)
PORT_CODE_DEC(KEYCODE_Z) PORT_CODE_INC(KEYCODE_X) PORT_PLAYER(1)

A relatively small change, but it makes the controls work intuitively
right from the start.

What really surprised me was how easy it was to add controllers 3 and
4.  In addition to the knob line above, controller 1 is set up as follows:

    PORT_BIT( 0x01, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_JOYSTICK_UP) PORT_PLAYER(1)
PORT_8WAY
    PORT_BIT( 0x02, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_JOYSTICK_DOWN) PORT_PLAYER(1)
PORT_8WAY
    PORT_BIT( 0x04, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_JOYSTICK_LEFT) PORT_PLAYER(1)
PORT_8WAY
    PORT_BIT( 0x08, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_JOYSTICK_RIGHT) PORT_PLAYER(1)
PORT_8WAY
	PORT_BIT( 0x10, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_BUTTON1) PORT_PLAYER(1)
    PORT_BIT( 0x20, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_UNUSED )
    PORT_BIT( 0x40, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_UNUSED )
    PORT_BIT( 0x80, IP_ACTIVE_HIGH, IPT_UNUSED )

Note the lines that have PORT_PLAYER(1) at the end.  I copied this
code exactly, then changed each instance of PORT_PLAYER(1) to
PORT_PLAYER(3).  Voila...working player three controller!  So the
ports were already set up correctly, the driver just didn't bother to
set the controls.

I'm sure adding Blue RAM support wouldn't be this easy, but I bet it
would be possible for someone who knew what they were doing.  Myself,
I would like to work on getting the ICBM Attack controller supported.
 I think I understand it well enough, but I'm not quite sure how
optional controllers should be added.

Paul

If you check back into The Arcadian newsletter you'll find that
NEITHER Blue Ram or Viper sold cheep! In fact the prices of ANY
memory expansion (64K Ram board included) was about the same, $250.00
more or less. The difference was in what was offered. Blue Ram came
with the basic on cartridge which allowed 15K of usable space for
your basic program (if you knew how)in a 16K unit. Whereas Viper came
with the basic on a tape using 8K of ram to reside in, leaving only
7K of usable space for your basic program also in a 16K unit. Viper
also came with a couple of demo programs (I believe the Viper Test
Pattern was one of those), whereas Blue Ram came with a tape that had
Blue Ram Utility and Artillery Duel! The latter became a cartridge,
but the owners of Blue Ram's could play the game long before
Astrocade released it (I DID!)! The former was a work in progress so
to speak and versions exhist in various stages of development. This
program allows editing of hex code, testing a game cartridge,
dissasembly of a machine code program, swaping, inserting, modem
software, a printer driver that prints out hex or assembly code, a
cartridge copy routine, a burner driver for up to 8K EPROMS, and a
few other "goodies" such as a routine that does something of what
Adam was asking about. The "unpack" command allows you to take a
basic program written and saved in Astro Basic and change formats so
that it can run in BRB (with some changes, such as the sound
variables and scroll modes). When Ken gets this program ready to go
it may not have everything I just mentioned because some of those
features use an 8154 Duel IO and LILL' WHITE RAM doesn't have that.

There's more than one multi-cart, and I can't speak for any but the one
I once made ... but in general, the files chosen for inclusion on that
thing were ones that came from an informal, three-way collaborative
effort. The Real Mike White (tm) had been saving all sorts of things,
from pretty much the dawn of (the Astrocade's) time. Adam and Mike were
in touch pretty often, and they were in charge of keeping track of the
library: all sorts of historical details that would have been (and
mostly still are) "over my head". Names of who-did-what; dates; etc.

My two cents was basically acting as a system translator: I would copy
carts or chips or whatever, that Adam or Mike loaned me: so that it
moved from an Astrocade-only format, to a PC-compatible one. I'd make
sure Adam had PC-readable copies, and from time to time (as I recall it
now, anyway) would send chips to Mike, so he could read them and make
sure I was doing each file just right. (I'm thinking if that happened
extensively, it would have been the BasicCart stuff?) I didn't ever see
myself as the big "techno-historical" expert on the Bally cart library:
that's Adam and Mike's department! (With tapes being another whopper of
a project, that I had zip to do with.) I don't mean to imply I didn't
care about things, by any means! -- I wanted to have things exactly
right -- but it's only fair for me to point my fingers at them, as The
Most Infinitely Wise and Wonderful Head Internet Elves (tm); since it
was them I relied on to make sure things were as kosher as possible.

For the record: one reason Adam and Ward and Mike got along easily is
that we're all of the opinion that programs SHOULDN'T be altered, by
anyone but the person that originally created them! Hacked or trained
or whatever copies, were not going to be good enough, in our eyes.

Let's face it: the Astrocade's pretty darn cool. But I had my head (and
hard drives) full of info about the Commodore VIC-20 home computer, at
the time I was doing any Bally archiving / system-translation work; so
I sort of showed up when called; did my thing; and then went and did
stuff on the Arcadia 2001 (and it's thirty thousand freakin' global
clones) afterwards. The multi-cart work was done, obviously, during the
peak in my Bally-related activities. Then I "retired" for five years.

As far as any chicken-and-the-egg stuff goes: Adam and Mike's careful
work preceeded my multi-cart; and was/is still around, after it. So, if
Adam or Mike (or their helpers-of-today) vouches for things, file-wise:
that's Golden Gospel as far as I'm concerned!

I hope that helped ... instead of confusing things worse!?

  -- Ward Shrake --
